title: Gareth B. Matthews, The Child's Philosopher; Maughn Rollins Gregory and Megan Jane Laverty, eds.; Routledge, 2021, Pp. 278.
authors: Gregory Lewis Bynum
abstract: Gareth B. Matthews, The Child's Philosopher, a volume in the Philosophy for Children Founders series, is a wonderful book that does not admit of easy summary. Its well-conceived, rich, and diverse perspectives, in an essay collection alternating the writings of philosopher Gareth B. Matthews with articles by scholars responding to his work, bear repeated study and consideration. Responses to this book can — and, I hope, will — open out in many directions. Its themes include the following: Matthews's work aimed at cultivating free and open philosophical communication with children that has intellectual value by the standards of professional philosophy; philosophically valuable discussions and the partaking in “philosophical whimsy” that emerge in and from books written for children; continuities and discontinuities between the Philosophy for Children movement (hereafter referred to as “Philosophy for Children”) and the history of philosophy; the question of whether Philosophy for Children sufficiently opposes politically oppressive social hierarchies and respectfully engages with cultural diversity; the different roles and strengths of Philosophy for Children founders, including Matthews, Ann Margaret Sharp, and Matthew Lipman; potential connections between Philosophy for Children and a Wittgenstein-inspired improved attention to “the ordinary” and to related “outbreaks of our childhood” that people experience throughout life;1 Philosophy for Children as liberatory, opposing oppressive and inaccurate “deficit models” of children's intellectual and artistic achievement and potential; and problems arising in efforts to understand the concepts “children” and “childhood.” Of the book's many themes, I will emphasize two: (1) perspectives on developmental psychology, and (2) issues of gender connected to Philosophy for Children. I have long loved Philosophy for Children and presented it, to very positive student response, in my Educational Foundations classes. For me, thinking and teaching about the movement have been associated with emphatic rejection of accounts of childhood intellect in (now largely discredited) Piagetian stage theory and other similar ways of thinking about human developmental stages by thinkers such as Aristotle, Jean-Jacques Rousseau, John Rawls, and Lawrence Kohlberg2 — ways of thinking where children are inaccurately undervalued as being incapable of reasoning, making moral judgments, identifying cause-effect connections, and understanding when another person's perspective differs from their own. Relatedly, I am sympathetic to Matthews, who critiqued the way Piagetian-style stage theory undesirably promotes condescension toward children, excessive othering of children, and eagerness to push children to supposedly “grow beyond their current stage” instead of rightly appreciating children's mental quality of openness to perplexity and wonderment.3 Matthews emphasizes children's often unrealized potential to discuss, beautifully, a range of challenging philosophical topics including death, bravery, honesty, difficulties in attributing causality, what it means to live a happy life, distinctions between nature and culture, experiences of being asleep and dreaming, and the question of whether the universe has a boundary. Furthermore, he presents a compelling argument that resisting stage theory's errors is a moral imperative: the imperative to see, value, and respect not only children's intellect but also children's capacity for moral insight, moral judgment, and moral agency.4 This imperative is also a social justice imperative to fully respect children's fundamental human rights and human value. In Philosophy for Children, this improved and fuller valuing of children occurs both through the understanding of children that the movement espouses and through educators engaging in philosophical dialogue with children. My experience reading this book, while not invalidating the criticisms of stage theory, did helpfully broaden and complicate my thinking about it. It helped me better understand (1) the appeal of stage theory, which has been massively influential historically, and (2) why one element of stage theory — its view of childhood mental life as distinct from adult mental life — remains important for thinking about childhood intellect in a range of contexts, including Philosophy for Children. For many, stage theory has supported a humane rejection of the traditional view of children as being nothing but deficient adults. Stage theory has validated a conceptual separation between childhood and adulthood, possibly protecting childhood from being inappropriately judged by adult standards.5 While, as has been noted, Matthews opposed stage theory in the tradition of Piaget and Rousseau, he nonetheless employed a kind of developmental-stages-based thinking when he observed that children of different ages tend to respond differently in philosophical discussions of children's literature. Younger children, according to him, are more likely to see ironic stories as serious thought experiments and to be “philosophically intrigued by fantastical stories involving violent or unseemly details, which adults often dismiss as nonsense.”6 Matthews also observed other positive, distinctive features of people at the childhood stage of human development: according to him they are “more imaginative; they give strikingly original and detailed examples; they are willing to seriously entertain thought experiments; and they are more sensitive to the complexities of human motivation.”7 Further, he thought that “very often children are much more sensitive to what is philosophically interesting and philosophically problematic than adults are,” and that children, in their thinking, may have “a kind of spontaneity,” “directness,” and “vividness” from which “adults can profit” by returning to reflection on essential questions of life that are unresolvable, or not easily resolvable.8 Children also may be better at entering into “the wonder that Plato and Aristotle identified as the beginning of philosophy.”9 Indeed, a kind of developmental-stages-based thinking is present in Matthews's “mirror image” conception of the relationship between a child and an adult engaged in a philosophical discussion — a conception in which each brings something distinct that the other, by virtue of their developmental stage of life, lacks.10 In his account, children are generally superior in the areas just mentioned (imagination, spontaneity, vividness of thought, etc.), while adults are generally superior in some important areas of knowledge and skill (knowledge of social conventions, familiarity with intellectual traditions, practice reflecting on certain philosophical problems, etc.). At the same time, in his view philosophical dialogue between adults and children ultimately most markedly brings out a sense of continuity, rather than disjunction, between childhood and adult phases of experience. In the beautiful wording of Stephanie Burdick-Shepherd and Christina Cammarano, Matthews calls us to realize that “the need to think philosophically is inherent to humans, from early childhood through advanced adulthood.”11 Among this book's statements about gender, some of the most provocative are about male gendered experience. Matthews analogized the liberation of men from the false superiority of sexism to the liberation of adults, through philosophical conversation with children, from the false superiority of ageism (the bias of assuming adult intellect to be superior to child intellect), and from the false pose of adult omniscience that so often impedes adult-child relationships12 — problems of false superiority that, due to sexism, seem more likely to afflict male adults than female adults. And, of course, the afflicted in this oppressive relationship also include those placed in the position of false inferiority: the children. As Karin Murris suggests in her chapter, it is possible that adult-authored discourse directed at children, including philosophical discussion directed at children by adults, could oppress or even colonize the children; after all, the conventions of professional philosophy and the framing of its problems have largely been devised to serve the perspective of adult white male philosophers.13 This may call into question the possibility of what Laverty and Gregory describe as Matthews's “transdisciplinary and age-transgressive approach to philosophizing in which the playing field between children and adults is leveled”14 — such a leveling cannot happen in a relationship where adults oppress children. The important questions that Matthews and Murris raise about the gender-differentiated oppression of adults, the oppression of children, and whether philosophy counters or perpetuates those oppressions require further examination. Perhaps the strongest and most coherent way forward is to inquire not only into adults' and children's experiences of oppression, but also into how oppression experienced in childhood may influence adult experience, causing adult experience to be oppressive as well, and further, to inquire how childhood experiences of oppression can best be understood and decreased or even eliminated, thereby potentially decreasing or eliminating adult experiences of oppression. For the purpose of understanding the essential nature of childhood experiences of oppression, and especially oppressive experiences that impede or prevent the human education and growth which leads to what the Universal Declaration of Human Rights calls “the full development of the human personality,” a 2000 study is especially suggestive. The study, titled “Gender Bias in Mothers' Expectations about Infant Crawling,” involved mothers being invited to set an adjustable ramp at an angle appropriate for challenging their crawling babies.15 The mothers of male babies set the ramp at too steep an angle for their babies to crawl down, while the mothers of female babies set the ramp at an angle that was less steep than their babies could have handled. In other words, the mothers overestimated the male babies' potential while underestimating their limitations, and they underestimated the female babies' potential while overestimating their limitations.16 This representation of oppressive and miseducative differential treatment of overrated males whose limitations are disrespected and underrated females whose limitations are exaggerated can helpfully (hypothetically) be taken as a conceptual template for understanding a wide range of oppressive and miseducative social phenomena. It is useful not only for understanding the oppression of males and females, and the related oppression of gender nonbinary people who are inappropriately pressured to conform to traditionally masculine and feminine roles, but also for understanding spheres of social activity traditionally deemed “masculine,” such as academic philosophy, and spheres of social activity traditionally deemed “feminine,” such as childrearing. This suggests the question, what happens when the traditionally “feminine” sphere of childrearing and the traditionally “masculine” sphere of academic philosophy come together in Philosophy for Children? Related to the dangers that stem from “feminizing” underestimation of human potential and overestimation of human limitations, philosophical discussion, with its forays into questions of the unknown and its embrace of challenging disagreements and debates, may alienate traditionally minded childhood educators who, underestimating childhood intellectual potential, think adults' education of children should be confined to what is certainly knowable — unambiguously teaching children basic facts, basic skills, and “right from wrong.” Note that Philosophy for Children scholar and educator Catherine C. McCall, while highly valuing the sense of wonder that Philosophy for Children can invoke, has commented that “for many adults, the discovery of wonder is quite scary.”17 And Philosophy for Children founder Matthew Lipman, who particularly focused on bringing Philosophy for Children into schools, described Philosophy for Children as aiming for “a major change in the nature of education,” specifically, a shift away from excessively limiting children's intellectual lives and toward an education centered on democracy-supporting critical “thinking rather than rote learning”; he notes that this form of education constitutes preparation “for a very different kind of world.”18 What about the converse dangers of miseducation, suggested by the mothers' making the ramp too steep for their crawling male babies, from “masculinizing” overestimation of human potential and disrespectful underestimation of human limitations and vulnerabilities — dangers that Karin Murris points to when she mentions the possibility of adults, and adult thinking, “colonizing” children through adult-authored children's literature and through the use of children's literature in Philosophy for Children?19 This concern may prompt consideration of how, in philosophical discussion, there can be needlessly hurtful, and intellectually unhelpful, overemphasis on personalized conflicts in the form of debates, intellectual contests, or clashes of schools of thought where some people become “winners” and other people become “losers.” Related to this, I confess to feeling uncomfortable while watching a videotaped Philosophy for Children class where a teacher summarized young children's expression of diverse ideas about the nature of thinking as a set of personal disagreements. The teacher summed up one child's contribution to the discussion as follows: “you agree with Joanna that your brain thinks, and you don't agree with Clarissa who said it's you that thinks.”20 I wonder if the interest of the contrast between differing views could have more usefully been brought out in a depersonalized way, perhaps through a repetition of the children's contrasting ideas without naming the children who expressed the different ideas. Through this depersonalized approach — an approach that could be described as fostering critical deliberation rather than debate — perhaps a child who expresses an idea that is the opposite of an idea expressed by a second child could, with greater ease and without the distraction of feeling drawn into a personal contest with someone else, freely consider the potential validity of the second child's view, thereby more greatly and readily expanding their own sense and understanding of the problem under discussion. Contrary to what is often assumed in the cultures of academe, historically dominated by an ideology of “masculinity,” personalized competition may sometimes be an impediment, rather than a stimulus, to students' intellectual growth and intellectual achievement. In my own teaching, I have often asked my students to make a presentation in class where they provide both a summary of a philosophical argument and a contrasting view opposed to that argument. This allows my students and me to enjoy together, and to profit intellectually from, the interplay of contrasting ideas without our feelings and thoughts about our discussion topic being distorted or pushed aside by more narrowly personal feelings of triumph, exaltation, disappointment, and mortification. If I am right that gender biases can fundamentally impede, or even prevent, success in Philosophy for Children classes and in education generally, this leads to the question, what can be done to counter gender bias in education? It seems to me that a good answer may be found in Matthews's focus on story-based teaching and philosophical whimsy and in a focus on humor related to philosophical whimsy in philosophical conversations with children. Providing a beautiful example that unites these things — and one that seems to me to be free from the harms gender bias can produce — Matthews describes adult-child communication on the philosophical theme of difficulties in the attribution of causality engaged through an adult and a child reading together, and sharing responses to, Arnold Lobel's children's book, Frog and Toad Together.21 In the story, Toad is anxious to be a successful gardener, and he's worried that the seeds he has planted won't grow. In an effort to make them grow, Toad plays music for them and reads them poetry. When, in the end, Frog congratulates Toad on the sprouted seeds, Toad remarks that making the seeds grow was “very hard work” — a statement that provokes laughter from the child hearing the story, who remarks to the adult that the playing of music and the reading of poetry were not really what caused the seeds to grow.22 This enables shared insight, between the adult and the child, into the fact (a fact frequently evident in all-adult communication) that it often can be easy to make mistakes in attributing cause-effect connections. The interaction exemplifies valuable respect for a child's capacity to understand this complex problem related to causality, and it serves as an important counterexample to starting from the false assumption that the child's intellect is too limited to understand causality and the challenges of thinking about causality (a fundamental false assumption of Piagetian stage theory). At the same time, insight is developed without recourse to needlessly competitive, combative, over-exalting, triumphalist, demoralizing, or mortifying discourse; insight is developed humorously and organically in communication where the main foci are (1) enjoying a good story, and (2) the sometime difficulty of securely identifying cause-effect connections. While this may provide one effective response to the gender bias problem, it is important to ask this: What else can be done to counter the deleterious intellectual, emotional, and educational effects title: Why we need to be careful with LLMs in medicine.
authors: Jean-Christophe Bélisle-Pipon
abstract: Large language models (LLMs), the core of many generative AI (genAI) tools, are gaining attention for their potential applications in healthcare. These applications are wide-ranging, including tasks such as assisting with diagnostic processes, streamlining patient communication, and providing decision support to healthcare professionals. Their ability to process and generate large volumes of text makes them promising tools for managing medical documentation and enhancing the efficiency of clinical workflows (Harrer, 2023). LLMs offer a distinct advantage in that they are relatively straightforward to use, particularly since the introduction of ChatGPT-3.5, and they exhibit a notable alignment with human language and communication patterns, facilitating more natural interactions (Ayers et al., 2023) and acceptance of the LLMs' conclusions (Shekar et al., 2024). LLMs operate by predicting the next word in a sequence based on statistical correlations identified in large datasets (Patil et al., 2021;Schubert et al., 2023). However, while these models are effective at producing text that appears coherent and contextually appropriate, they do so without a genuine understanding of meaning or context. This limitation is particularly significant in healthcare, where accuracy is critical. Unlike human cognition, which is driven by a complex array of goals and behaviors, LLMs are narrowly focused on text generation. This focus can lead to the production of plausible sounding but inaccurate information, a phenomenon referred to as "AI hallucination" (OpenAI et al., 2024). In high-stakes environments like prediction, triaging, diagnosis, monitoring, or patient care, these inaccuracies can have serious consequences.While numerous articles across various Frontiers journals discuss LLMs, relatively few focus on AI hallucinations as a central issue. For example, Jin et al. (2023) in Frontiers in Medicine note that "While LLMs like ChatGPT offer tremendous potential in ophthalmology, addressing the challenges of AI hallucination and misinformation is paramount." Similarly, Giorgino et al. (2023) in Frontiers in Surgery emphasize that "The responsible use of this tool must be based on an awareness of its limitations and biases. Foremost among these is the dangerous concept of AI hallucination." Beyond the realm of healthcare, Williams (2024) in Frontiers in Education observes that "The concept of AI hallucination gained widespread attention around 2022, coinciding with the rise of LLMs such as ChatGPT. Users noticed these chatbots often generated random falsehoods in their responses, seemingly indifferent to relevance or accuracy." Williams (2024) continues by stressing that the "term AI hallucination has been criticized for its anthropomorphic connotations, as it likens human perception to the behavior of language models." Despite these critical discussions, they remain sparse compared to the many articles praising LLMs in medicine, highlighting the need for greater engagement in addressing the limitations of these technologies. This imbalance highlights the need for greater emphasis on mitigating the risks posed by these models. Building on this concern, Hicks, Humphries, and Slater (2024) challenge conventional thinking in their paper "ChatGPT is Bullshit." They assert that the inaccuracies produced by LLMs should not simply be labeled as "hallucinations," but as "bullshit," a term based on philosopher Harry Frankfurt's (2009) work. According to this perspective, "bullshit" reflects a disregard for accuracy, which poses serious challenges for the use of genAI in healthcare. By reconceptualizing LLMs in healthcare as "bullshiting" instead of "hallucinating," this paper aims to provide a perspective on the risks these tools pose in critical applications. It explores practical solutions such as layered LLM architectures and improved XAI methods, and emphasizes the urgency of implementing tailored oversight mechanisms to counterbalance the political and industry push for AI deregulation in sensitive domains like medicine.LLMs generate text by predicting the next word based on large datasets. While they produce human-like text, they don't inherently understand or verify its accuracy, acting as "prop-oriented make-believe tools" (Mallory, 2023). Their errors are not the result of technical glitches that can be resolved with better data or refined algorithms but stem from their fundamental nature-they do not evaluate evidence or reason in the human sense. This critical distinction between LLMs' statistical processing and human reasoning can lead to misconceptions, particularly when LLMs are portrayed or perceived as capable of human-like cognition. While LLMs can generate accurate and contextually relevant text, their outputs are based on statistical correlations, not genuine comprehension. As Bender et al. (2021) famously argued, LLMs, which generate word sequences based on learned patterns, function as "stochastic parrots." In contrast, human reasoning involves deeper cognitive processes such as understanding, critical thinking, and interpretation. While some, like Downes et al. (2024), challenge this view, suggesting that LLMs can produce sensible answers by leveraging higher-level structural information inherent in their design, the fact remains that LLMs remain fundamentally agnostic to empirical reality. Recognizing this distinction is crucial, as the statistical predictions made by AI models-no matter how convincing-should not be equated with deliberate, evidence-based reasoning of the human mind. When these AI systems make mistakes, it is not because they are malfunctioning in a way that can be fixed with better data or tweaked algorithms. It is because they fundamentally do not arbitrate evidence in the first place. As Hicks et al. (2024) point out: "ChatGPT is not trying to communicate something they believe or perceive. Their inaccuracy is not due to misperception or hallucination. As we have pointed out, they are not trying to convey information at all. They are bullshitting." This indifference to evidence is especially concerning in medicine, where accuracy, interpretability, and liability are paramount. Consider the implications of using genAI to provide medical advice or assist in diagnosing patients-if the nature of its outputs is misunderstood, it poses significant risks. Trusting and acting on potentially flawed information could result in misdiagnoses and improper treatments, with serious consequences for patient care. As stated by Harrer (2023): "Health buyers beware: generative AI is an experimental technology not yet ready for primetime."Recognizing that these AI systems produce "bullshit" rather than "hallucinations" calls for a more cautious and skeptical approach, according to Hicks and colleagues. Titus (2024) convincingly stated that "Attributing semantic understanding to these systems when we are not warranted in doing so could have serious social and ethical implications related to anthropormorphizing (sic) these systems or over-trusting their ability to produce meaningful or truthful responses." In the health sector, this implies that, mMedical professionals should be wary about them and avoid using LLMs as standalone sources of information or advice (Cohen, 2023). Instead, LLMs should serve as supplementary tools, with all outputs rigorously validated by human experts before being applied and used in any clinical setting. The ethical implications of using AI in medicine are significant. If AI systems are inherently indifferent to the truth, there is a heightened responsibility on developers and users to ensure these tools do not cause harm. This involves not only improving the technical accuracy of AI models but also clearly communicating their limitations to users. As Hicks et al (2024) note, "Calling chatbot inaccuracies 'hallucinations' feeds into overblown hype about their abilities among technology cheerleaders, and could lead to unnecessary consternation among the general public. It also suggests solutions to the inaccuracy problems which might not work, and could lead to misguided efforts at AI alignment amongst specialists." Given the significant ethical implications of AI in medicine, LLMs should be used as supplementary tools with expert validation of both medical AI design and outputs prior to clinical applications (Bélisle-Pipon et al., 2021;Cohen, 2023).Ensuring AI trustworthiness in healthcare requires shared responsibility, with developers creating transparent systems and medical professionals critically assessing AI outputs and their limitations (Amann et al., 2020;Díaz-Rodríguez et al., 2023;Siala & Wang, 2022;Smith, 2021). Medical professionals must be trained to understand that AI-generated content that may sound convincing, is not always reliable. Developers should prioritize creating interfaces that highlight these limitations and encourage critical evaluation of AI outputs. For example, including disclaimers or confidence scores can help users better assess the reliability of the information provided (Gallifant et al., 2024). This is basically what the Notice and Explanation section of the the White House's AI Bill of Rights (2022) requires: "Medical professionals should not use AI as a standalone source of information or advice. Instead, AI should serve as a supplementary tool, with all outputs rigorously validated by human experts before being applied in any clinical setting." However, disclosure is not enough in itself as it is also conducive to problems, particularly by shifting the burden onto users. Such disclosure should be accessible and understandable in a way that does not reproduce the problems of consumer products' Terms and Conditions, which are made ridiculously long to ensure that nobody reads them (Solove, 2024).Employing multiple layers of LLMs to mitigate the limitations inherent in individual models could be a way to solve the previously raised issues. Work is currently underway in this area (Farquhar et al., 2024). Usually this entails enabling one model to cross-validate the outputs of another to identify and correct inaccuracies, thereby reducing the incidence of AI hallucination. This layered approach, wherein different models are assigned specialized tasks such as factchecking or contextual validation, has the potential to enhance the robustness and reliability of AI-generated content (Springer, 2024). However, this methodology introduces significant complexity, including the risk of error propagation and the challenges associated with the coordination of multiple models. Furthermore, while this strategy, which Verspoor (2024) calls "fighting fire with fire," may incrementally improve the accuracy of outputs, it fails to address the foundational issue of LLMs' lack of true semantic understanding. An over-reliance on layered LLMs could result in diminishing returns, where the added complexity and potential for novel errors negate the anticipated benefits of enhanced accuracy. Additionally, this approach risks fostering an overdependence on AI systems (Levinstein & Herrmann, 2024), potentially undermining the role of human expertise in domains requiring nuanced understanding and ethical decision-making.LLMs can still offer valuable contributions to medical practice if used wisely. LLMs can assist in administrative tasks, generate patient documentation, or provide preliminary information on medical topics. They can even be useful in defending patients' interests in health insurance claims (Rosenbluth, 2024). However, these applications must be designed with safeguards to prevent over-reliance on potentially inaccurate outputs (Cohen, 2023). One way to enhance LLMs' utility in medicine is not to rely solely on them, but also to implement verification systems based on reliable databases (not just web-scrapping). Even Hicks et al. (2024) emphasize that there are practical solutions to address the concerns of AI "bullshit." For example, connecting a LLM to a trusted medical database can help ensure the information it provides is cross-referenced with reliable sources. Such a system would also incorporate a mechanism for arbitrating evidence, further enhancing accuracy and providing a certain level of trustworthiness. However, this integration must be implemented carefully to avoid introducing new forms of misinformation or inadvertently embedding values that are inconsistent with the context in which the tool is being deployed (Bélisle-Pipon et al., 2021).Explainable AI (XAI) aims to increase transparency in AI decision-making, including in LLMs. Techniques like attention mechanisms and post-hoc explanations help users understand how AI generates outputs, especially in high-stakes fields like healthcare. However, XAI does not address the core limitation: LLMs depend on statistical patterns, not genuine reasoning or evidence evaluation (Titus, 2024). Moreover, while these techniques are valuable for tracing outputs back to their underlying processes, they often fail to expose the deeper epistemic limitations of LLMs, such as their inability to reason or evaluate evidence. Their explanations, therefore, reflect these patterns rather than any meaningful understanding. Regulatory frameworks, such as the European Union's AI Regulation ( 2024) and the US AI Bill of Rights Blueprint (The White House, 2022), establish critical standards for transparency, safety, and accountability. However, adapting LLMs to meet these standards may not overcome their fundamental limitations in reasoning and evidence-based decision-making. Experts argue for shifting focus from refining LLMs to developing new AI paradigms, such as neurosymbolic AI, which combines neural networks with logical reasoning to address these gaps.Neurosymbolic AI offers a promising alternative, integrating neural adaptability with logical precision to enable more robust reasoning and contextual understanding (Hamilton et al., 2024;Wan et al., 2024). These models can potentially overcome key limitations of LLMs, offering greater efficiency and interpretability. As Vivek Wadhwa (2024) suggests, LLMs are nearing their developmental ceiling, and further investment in them risks diminishing returns. Instead, regulators and investors may explore advancing neurosymbolic AI to drive the next generation of innovation, while ensuring AI systems are both transparent and capable of increased trustworthy reasoning. Despite its promise, neurosymbolic AI is not a panacea. It faces challenges in scalability, interpretability, and handling the complexity of real-world medical data (Marra et al., 2024). Moreover, its reliance on logical structures may not fully capture the nuances of probabilistic and ambiguous information common in medicine. Thus, while neurosymbolic AI represents an incremental advance, robust oversight, multidisciplinary collaboration, and continued innovation remain essential for addressing AI's limitations in critical domains like healthcare.A deep, critical examination of the inherent limitations of LLMs is crucial for advancing medical AI in ways that prioritize patient safety and ethical integrity. While LLMs like ChatGPT can generate fluent, coherent text, this proficiency often conceals a more troubling reality: their responses are not necessarily grounded in verified facts or consistent logic. In the medical field, where evidence-based decision-making is paramount, relying on these models without addressing their fundamental flaws presents significant risks. LLMs, at their core, are probabilistic models designed to predict the next word in a sequence based on patterns in training data. This mechanism, though powerful for generating human-like text, is fundamentally indifferent to truth. If the goal of the model is to generate the most statistically likely response rather than the correct or most appropriate one, there is a significant risk of misinformation infiltrating clinical workflows.As Jin et al. (2023) underscore, "Responsible AI implementation and continuous monitoring are essential to harness the benefits of AI while minimizing potential risks." A key concern with LLMs in medical applications is their lack of reproducibility. Unlike traditional software systems, where identical inputs yield consistent outputs, LLMs can generate different answers to the same question on different occasions. This unpredictability undermines the reliability needed in medical settings, where consistency is essential for delivering safe and effective care. Medicine, as a discipline, cannot afford to embrace tools that exhibit "epistemic insouciance"-a disregard for the reliability and validity of knowledge. This is especially problematic given that LLMs, in many cases, are not anchored in factual reality but are designed to produce text that merely sounds plausible. The use of the term "hallucination" to describe when LLMs generate factually incorrect statements trivializes the severity of the issue. In truth, this behavior reflects a deeper problem: LLMs are trained to predict patterns, not to produce factual outputs. In medicine-an evidence-based practice since the 1990s-this fundamental flaw can lead to the adoption of unreliable tools that compromise the integrity of patient care.The standard disclaimers provided by models like ChatGPT, which warn that "ChatGPT can make mistakes. Check important info," are insufficient safeguards in clinical settings. While Harrer (2023) points out that "In defence of OpenAI, it never advertised ChatGPT as trustworthy advisor but rather as a crowdsourced technology evaluation and refinement experiment"; Harrer also acknowledged that there is insufficient risk mitigation across genAI, including ChatGPT, which has sparked growing caution amid internet-level hype. The implications for the health sector are significant, most users (especially Hhealthcare professionals) often lack the time or expertise to verify every piece of AI-generated information, especially in high-pressure stake environments where the margin for error is slim, but the consequences significant. Entrusting users with the responsibility of fact-checking AI outputs without giving them the resources or assurances of accuracy exposes the field to potentially dangerous mistakes, as well as to arguably lead to AI ethics dumping, so to offload such responsibility to downstream users (Bélisle-Pipon & Victor, 2024). The casual acceptance of these limitations in AI use-particularly in medicine, where errors can have life-threatening consequences-reflects a dangerous complacency. Transparency, interpretability, and trustworthiness in medical AI is are not a luxury but a necessity. Healthcare professionals need to understand not only what the AI recommends but also how and why it arrived at its conclusions. Explainability in AI systems is critical for building trust and enabling professionals to make informed decisions based on AI output. title: Precision in Prevention and Health Surveillance: How Artificial Intelligence May Improve the Time of Identification of Health Concerns through Social Media Content Analysis.
authors: Pascal Staccini, Annie Y S Lau, Findings from the Yearbook 2024 Section on Consumer Health Informatics
abstract:
<AbstractText Label="OBJECTIVE" NlmCategory="OBJECTIVE">To explore how artificial intelligence (AI) methodologies, particularly through the analysis of social media content, can enhance "precision in prevention and health surveillance" (2024 Yearbook topic). The focus is on leveraging advanced data analytics to improve the timeliness and accuracy of identifying emerging health concerns, thus enabling more proactive and effective health interventions.</AbstractText>
          <AbstractText Label="METHODS" NlmCategory="METHODS">A comprehensive literature search strategy was conducted on PubMed, focusing on papers published in 2023 related to consumer health informatics, precision prevention, and the intersection with social media. The search aimed to identify studies that utilized AI and machine learning techniques to analyse social media data for health surveillance purposes. Bibliometric analyses were applied to the retrieved articles, and tools such as "Bibliometrix" were used to assess keyword frequencies, co-occurrence networks, and thematic maps. The studies were then independently reviewed and screened for relevance, with a final selection of 10 articles made based on their alignment with the 2024 Yearbook topic and their methodological innovation.</AbstractText>
          <AbstractText Label="RESULTS" NlmCategory="RESULTS">The analysis of 89 articles revealed several key themes and findings. Social media data offers a rich source of real-time insights into public health trends, and encompasses diverse demographic groups. AI methodologies, including machine learning, natural language processing (NLP), and deep learning, play a crucial role in extracting and analysing health-related information from social media content. The integration of AI in health surveillance can provide early warnings of potential health crises, as demonstrated by studies on topics such as suicide prevention, mental health, and the impact of social media use on e-cigarette consumption among youth. Ethical and privacy considerations are paramount, necessitating robust data anonymization and transparent data handling practices. Advanced AI techniques, such as transformer-based topic modelling and federated learning, enhance the precision and security of health surveillance systems. The document highlights several case studies that demonstrate the practical applications of AI in health surveillance, such as monitoring public discussions about delta-8 THC and assessing suicide-related tweets and their association with help-seeking behaviour in the US.</AbstractText>
          <AbstractText Label="CONCLUSION" NlmCategory="CONCLUSIONS">Integrating AI and social media content analysis in precision prevention and health surveillance has significant potential to improve public health outcomes. By leveraging real-time, comprehensive data from social media platforms, AI can enhance the timeliness and accuracy of identifying health concerns. Addressing ethical and privacy challenges is crucial to ensure responsible and effective implementation. The continuous advancement of AI technologies will play a critical role in safeguarding public health and responding to emerging health threats.</AbstractText>

title: Faculty‐student authorship: Policy development
authors: Emily Eiswirth, Ann Miller
abstract: In academic settings, including nursing, scholarship expectations with the intent of publication are required of both faculty and students often under time constraints and excessive workloads. Successful scholarly completion is considered a measure of achievement for faculty and graduate students often associated with personal and professional rewards such as tenure and promotion, career advancement, and funding opportunities. In order to be a successful scholarly collaboration, guidelines in the form of policy can protect author teams and provide clarity and direction regarding authorship criteria and authorship order. For faculty, scholarship is integrated into newly hired tenure track roles and is expected to be achieved within established timeframes while teaching full time, developing/updating course content and advising and mentoring students. Academic positions are often dependent upon successful completion and presentation of such projects.1 These scholarly requirements for faculty are associated with professional credibility and career satisfaction. Moreover, there can be ongoing scholarly mandates for faculty to achieve after securing tenure status which may present similar challenges.1 For students at the graduate level, scholarship requirements are built into the curriculum with faculty approval and oversight. Students work with faculty mentors who advise, monitor progress toward completion, and possibly contribute to scholarly work, allowing for faculty-student authorship collaborations.3 Ongoing clarification of author roles and responsibilities early and often throughout the scholarly process can decrease author conflicts.2-8 The literature highlights faculty-student authorship among many disciplines, including accounting, psychology, chemistry, mental health, family relations and nursing with differing authorship guidelines.2-8 In nursing academia, a study found that faculty conflicted on criteria that warranted authorship.2 Some faculty agreed that authorship was warranted for editing and revising while others did not.2 Nursing faculty agreed that acquiring funding and completing the review of the literature warranted authorship credit while other disciplines discredited these criteria.2 Regardless of discipline, the inherent power differential between faculty and students in academia is a complex and critical issue that can have a significant implications for collaboration, ethical behavior, and quality of scholarship.2 This power differential arises from the faculty's position as the gatekeeper of academic opportunities leading to the potential for unethical behavior.2 Moreover, policy development supporting ethical practices for faculty-student authorship in nursing academia was recommended.2-4 Additionally, House & Seeman6 suggest education of faculty regarding responsible conduct of research which can augment both faculty-faculty and faculty-student authorship collaborations. While the importance of scholarship expectations among these disciplines was universal, there was disparity noted among the disciplines regarding authorship criteria and authorship order.2, 3 Collins, et al4 assert co-author with seniority take the lead author role, while House & Seeman6 suggest authorship credit decisions should be based on existing guidelines including American Chemical Society and other professional societies and journals. Furthermore, the student was designated as primary author and faculty as second author with outlined role expectations in the family relations discipline and nursing experts recommended signage of a memorandum stating authorship order and expected contributions from each author.8, 9 Regardless of the discipline, academic collaborative authorships can experience author conflicts.9 With the lack of recent literature in the last 10 years, the findings support the development and standardization of guidelines for collaborative authorship practices, specifically with regard to authorship criteria and authorship order. Authorship collaborations among faculty-faculty members both inside and outside the academic setting as well as faculty-student collaborations can be more effective partnerships if designed and guided by a policy that highlights these deficiencies while decreasing and ultimately preventing conflicts and disputes concerning authorship criteria and order. Development of authorship policy addressing authorship criteria and authorship order is essential for successful scholarly collaborations in nursing academia. The purpose of this project was to explore the presence of an authorship policy in nursing academic programs and subsequent development of a collaborative authorship policy. Our data collection for policy development was a review of academic institutions from comparable schools, including two private schools where the authors are employed. This included 17 Mercy colleges and universities and 28 Jesuit colleges and universities with a combined count of 45 academic institutions. Mercy and Jesuit schools are academic institutions with distinct religious affiliations and similar educational philosophies. Of the 45 academic institutions, 37 have a school of nursing. A systematic search process was conducted to collect data from each institution's website. First, each institution's website was accessed via a Google search. Second, the institution's homepage “search” feature was used to search for authorship-related terms, including authorship policy, authorship agreement, and authorship guidelines. Third, results of the search were reviewed for anything related to authorship policy. Lastly, the deans or directors from the 37 schools of nursing were emailed to request a copy of their authorship policy, if applicable. This resulted in four policies that were reviewed. Given the few policies that were found through these methods, a Google search of authorship policy at universities was conducted and a request on the American Association of Colleges of Nursing (AACN) discussion board asking for nursing faculty to share their faculty-student authorship policy was posted. The Google search yielded 11 policies and the AACN discussion board post yielded zero policies. Upon completion of our Internet search of the institutions, responses from deans or directors, responses from the AACN discussion board and a Google search, there were 15 institutions with an authorship policy. The policies were reviewed for the following six aspects: (1) outlining authorship criteria, (2) recommending when to discuss authorship, (3) procedure for dispute resolution, (4) guidance on faculty-student collaboration, (5) objective tool for determining authorship credit, and (6) objective tool for determining authorship order. Of the 15 institutions with an authorship policy, 15 discussed authorship criteria, 12 recommended when to discuss authorship, 12 provided a procedure for dispute resolution, six discussed guidance on faculty-student collaboration, one provided an objective tool for determining authorship credit, and zero provided an objective tool for determining authorship order. A summary of the findings was used to highlight common guidelines and best practices regarding authorship and faculty-student collaboration. Based on these findings, an authorship policy was drafted. The policy consisted of five headings, including authorship policy, authorship criteria, order of authorship, faculty-student collaboration, and dispute resolution. Under the first heading, the policy identifies who the policy applies to and the purpose of the policy. Under authorship criteria, the policy outlines the criteria that warrants authorship as defined by the International Committee for Medical Journal Editors and American Psychological Association.10-12 The order of authorship section provides a rubric on how to determine who deserves authorship and the order of authorship based on the author's contributions to scholarly activity. The faculty-student collaboration heading outlines the ethical practices that should be followed. Lastly, the policy ends with a discussion and guidelines on dispute resolution. See Figures 1 and 2 for the faculty-student authorship policy and contract for publication. Authorship policy. Contract regarding publication intent. A review of the literature showed the need for a faculty-student authorship policy in nursing academia. Nursing academic institutions were explored to identify a faculty-student authorship policy. The summary of findings in this project were consistent with the review of the literature in that a few academic institutions have an authorship policy that addresses faculty-student collaboration, and zero institutions use or developed an objective tool to assist with authorship discussions. Further exploration identified six common aspects in the authorship policies that were used to develop a faculty-student authorship policy for academic nursing programs. In addition to the six aspects found in the authorship policies, faculty-student collaboration was an additional aspect included in the policy. Addressing these criteria address the challenges and contribute to the fair attribution of authorship in faculty-student collaboration, including authorship disputes, credit and recognition, power imbalance, intellectual property rights, communication issues, and time commitment. Acknowledging these common conflicts in the authorship policy can ensure that ethical considerations, interdisciplinary collaborations, and the diverse nature of scholarship are taken into consideration. The implications of the policy can positively impact both faculty and students. These guidelines provide faculty with structure, clarity, and a framework for effective collaboration with students. Additional benefits for faculty include improved communication, efficient task allocation, mitigation of authorship disputes, and enhanced mentorship opportunities. Clear guidelines ensure that both faculty and students understand their roles, responsibilities, and expectations in scholarship or research minimizing potential conflicts. This ensures that each team member contributes in a meaningful way, optimizing the use of resources and time. This can create a structured mentorship environment where faculty can provide guidance and direction to students. Collaborating with students introduces faculty to new perspectives and innovative ideas. A transparent process for faculty-student collaboration can provide an environment for academic and personal development for the student. Participating in the research process under a transparent policy exposes students to various aspects of the research process, including literature review, data collection, analysis, and manuscript preparation. Successful collaboration and publication can increase a student's confidence in their capabilities that can extend into other endeavors. The contributions to scholarship can be advantageous for career opportunities, as well. Limitations of this research project include institutional implementation. The policy may need to be revised to align with the institution's current practices. The policy may require faculty discussion and training for integration in the institution. There may be faculty who disagree with publishing with students regardless of a policy or an objective tool. Additional limitations include a small sample size where only Mercy and Jesuit institutions were explored. Future research should assess the effectiveness of the policy in real-world scenarios and its impact on faculty-student collaborations. Collaborative authorships are essential to developing, synthesizing, and disseminating new knowledge for the growth and advancement of disciplines, particularly the nursing profession. Faculty-student collaborative authorships are designed to be effective interactive networks in nursing academia to foster intellectual growth through mutually agreed upon goals and benefits. Therefore, it is imperative that both parties resolve and ultimately prevent conflicts related to authorship. The initiation of authorship expectations, review of guidelines or authorship contracts, and documentation of contributions early in the authorship process are key to successful collaborations. Transparency and crucial communication can alleviate many stressors and anxiety related to complex topics and disciplinary norms regarding authorship. It is vital that this topic continues to be a key conversation in academia to support both the student and faculty collaborative scholarly works and endeavors. The data used in this study is available upon request. Interested parties are invited to contact the corresponding author Emily Eiswirth via email at [email protected] to obtain access to the dataset. We are committed to facilitating transparency and collaboration in research and will respond promptly to requests for data sharing. Please note that access to the data is subject to compliance with ethical and privacy considerations, and requests will be evaluated on a case-by-case basis. She is an assistant professor at Loyola University New Orleans. Currently, she holds a position within a Federally Qualified Health Center where she plays a crucial role in ensuring access to affordable, high-quality healthcare for individuals and families, particularly those with limited financial resources or living in medically underserved communities. Ann Miller, DNP, MSN, APRN/CCNS, CCRN-K, earned a Doctor of Nursing Practice (DNP) degree from Governors State University in 2011. She is a certified acute care advanced practice nurse specializing in Critical Care and Cardiology. She is currently a full-time assistant professor in the College of Nursing at St. Xavier University in Chicago, IL.

title: ET: Explain to Train: Leveraging Explanations to Enhance the Training of A Multimodal Transformer
authors: Meghna P Ayyar, Jenny Benois-Pineau, Akka Zemmari
venue: 2024 IEEE International Conference on Image Processing (ICIP)
abstract: Explainable Artificial Intelligence (XAI) has become increasingly vital for improving the transparency and reliability of neural network decisions. Transformer architectures have emerged as the state-of-the-art for various tasks across single modalities such as video, language, or signals, as well as for multimodal approaches. Although XAI methods for transformers are available, their potential impact during model training remains underexplored. Thus, we propose Explanation-guided Training (ET), leveraging an XAI method to identify salient input regions and guide the model to focus solely on these salient regions during training. We develop ET in a typical multimodal analysis framework using a multimodal transformer that operates on videos and signals. ET enhances the input by masking the non-salient regions for videos and enhances the signals with weights based on explanation scores for the sensor modality. Comparative evaluation with baseline vanilla training and the state-of-the-art XAI-based IFI method [1] shows that ET consistently outperforms them. We benchmark our method on the publicly available UCF50 video dataset to demonstrate that ET is better than vanilla training and IFI. A risk detection corpus comprising egocentric videos and wearable sensor data is used for multimodal evaluation. Our code is available at https://gitub.u-bordeaux.fr/mayyar/explain-to-train

title: Impact of the COVID-19 pandemic on lung cancer diagnosis in northern Poland-addressing the COVID-19 debt.
authors: Anna Romaszko-Wojtowicz, Anna Doboszyńska, Anna Piechnik, Krzysztof Kuziemski, Dariusz Szplit, Szczepan Cofta, Katarzyna Glińska-Lewczuk
abstract:
<AbstractText Label="INTRODUCTION" NlmCategory="BACKGROUND">Lung cancer, one of the leading causes of death due to neoplasms, requires prompt diagnosis and immediate treatment. The COVID-19 pandemic affected healthcare systems worldwide, having adverse effects on all aspects, particularly on the fate of patients with suspected neoplastic diseases. Limited access to healthcare, disruptions in regular operations (reassigning roles to some wards), postponed hospital admissions, prolonged diagnostic processes, and other factors have collectively led to the phenomenon known as COVID-19 debt.</AbstractText>
          <AbstractText Label="MATERIAL AND METHODS" NlmCategory="METHODS">A retrospective analysis covered statistical data concerning the diagnosis of lung cancer obtained from three centres in northern Poland (Olsztyn, Bydgoszcz, Gdansk) and concerning years 2016 to 2022. Relative risks (RR) with 95% confidence intervals (CI) for cancer event were calculated. Before the pandemic, these centers prioritized the diagnosis of suspected lung cancer cases, which was subsequently disrupted during the pandemic due to various factors.</AbstractText>
          <AbstractText Label="RESULTS" NlmCategory="RESULTS">The COVID-19 pandemic led to a decrease in diagnosed lung cancer cases, especially in hospitals repurposed for COVID-19 care. A statistically significant trend in lung cancer incidence per 100,000 inhabitants was observed specifically in healthcare centers that maintained normal operations without disruption.</AbstractText>
          <AbstractText Label="CONCLUSION" NlmCategory="CONCLUSIONS">The concept of the COVID debt helps explain changes in lung cancer diagnosis during and post-pandemic, highlighting the need for increased public awareness and intensified diagnostic efforts to facilitate earlier disease detection.</AbstractText>

title: Mechanistic interpretability of large language models with applications to the financial services industry
authors: Ashkan Golgoon, Khashayar Filom, Arjun Ravi Kannan
venue: Proceedings of the 5th ACM International Conference on AI in Finance
abstract: Large Language Models exhibit remarkable capabilities across a broad spectrum of applications. Nevertheless, due to their intrinsic complexity, these models present substantial challenges in interpreting their internal decision-making processes. This lack of transparency poses critical challenges when it comes to their adaptation by financial institutions, where concerns and accountability regarding bias, fairness, and reliability are of paramount importance. Mechanistic interpretability aims at reverse engineering complex AI models such as transformers. In this paper, we are pioneering the use of mechanistic interpretability to shed some light on the inner workings of large language models for use in financial services applications. We offer several examples of how algorithmic tasks can be designed for compliance monitoring purposes. In particular, we investigate GPT-2 Small’s attention pattern when prompted to identify potential violation of Fair Lending laws. Using direct logit attribution, we study the contributions of each layer and its corresponding attention heads to the logit difference in the residual stream. Finally, we design clean and corrupted prompts and use activation patching as a causal intervention method to localize our task completion components further. We observe that the (positive) heads 10.2 (head 2, layer 10), 10.7, and 11.3, as well as the (negative) heads 9.6 and 10.6 play a significant role in the task completion.

title: The Implications of ChatGPT For Legal Services and Society
authors: Andrew Perlman
abstract:
<jats:p>On November 30, 2022, OpenAI released a chatbot called ChatGPT.1 To demonstrate the chatbot’s sophistication and its potential implications, both for legal services and society more generally, most of this paper was generated in about an hour through prompts within ChatGPT. Only this abstract, the preface, the outline headers, the footnotes, the epilogue, and the prompts were written by a person. ChatGPT generated the rest of the text with no human editing. To be clear, the responses generated by ChatGPT were imperfect and at times problematic, and the use of an AI tool for law-related services raises a host of regulatory and ethical issues. At the same time, ChatGPT highlights the promise of artificial intelligence, including its ability to affect our lives in both modest and more profound ways. ChatGPT suggests an imminent reimagination of how we access and create information, obtain legal and other services, and prepare people for their careers. We also will soon face new questions about the role of knowledge workers in society, the attribution of work (e.g., determining when people’s written work is their own), and the potential misuse of and excessive reliance on the information produced by these kinds of tools.

The disruptions from AI’s rapid development are no longer in the distant future. They have arrived, and this document offers a small taste of what lies ahead.</jats:p>

title: Ethical use of artificial intelligence to prevent sudden cardiac death: an interview study of patient perspectives.
authors: Menno T Maris, Ayca Koçar, Dick L Willems, Jeannette Pols, Hanno L Tan, Georg L Lindinger, Marieke A R Bak
abstract:
<AbstractText Label="BACKGROUND">The emergence of artificial intelligence (AI) in medicine has prompted the development of numerous ethical guidelines, while the involvement of patients in the creation of these documents lags behind. As part of the European PROFID project we explore patient perspectives on the ethical implications of AI in care for patients at increased risk of sudden cardiac death (SCD).</AbstractText>
          <AbstractText Label="AIM">Explore perspectives of patients on the ethical use of AI, particularly in clinical decision-making regarding the implantation of an implantable cardioverter-defibrillator (ICD).</AbstractText>
          <AbstractText Label="METHODS">Semi-structured, future scenario-based interviews were conducted among patients who had either an ICD and/or a heart condition with increased risk of SCD in Germany (n = 9) and the Netherlands (n = 15). We used the principles of the European Commission's Ethics Guidelines for Trustworthy AI to structure the interviews.</AbstractText>
          <AbstractText Label="RESULTS">Six themes arose from the interviews: the ability of AI to rectify human doctors' limitations; the objectivity of data; whether AI can serve as second opinion; AI explainability and patient trust; the importance of the 'human touch'; and the personalization of care. Overall, our results reveal a strong desire among patients for more personalized and patient-centered care in the context of ICD implantation. Participants in our study express significant concerns about the further loss of the 'human touch' in healthcare when AI is introduced in clinical settings. They believe that this aspect of care is currently inadequately recognized in clinical practice. Participants attribute to doctors the responsibility of evaluating AI recommendations for clinical relevance and aligning them with patients' individual contexts and values, in consultation with the patient.</AbstractText>
          <AbstractText Label="CONCLUSION">The 'human touch' patients exclusively ascribe to human medical practitioners extends beyond sympathy and kindness, and has clinical relevance in medical decision-making. Because this cannot be replaced by AI, we suggest that normative research into the 'right to a human doctor' is needed. Furthermore, policies on patient-centered AI integration in clinical practice should encompass the ethics of everyday practice rather than only principle-based ethics. We suggest that an empirical ethics approach grounded in ethnographic research is exceptionally well-suited to pave the way forward.</AbstractText>

title: CNNs trained with adult data are useful in pediatrics. A pneumonia classification example.
authors: Maria Rollan-Martinez-Herrera, Alejandro A Díaz, Rubén San José Estépar, Gonzalo Vegas Sanchez-Ferrero, James C Ross, Raúl San José Estépar, Pietro Nardelli
abstract:
<AbstractText Label="BACKGROUND AND OBJECTIVES" NlmCategory="OBJECTIVE">The scarcity of data for training deep learning models in pediatrics has prompted questions about the feasibility of employing CNNs trained with adult images for pediatric populations. In this work, a pneumonia classification CNN was used as an exploratory example to showcase the adaptability and efficacy of such models in pediatric healthcare settings despite the inherent data constraints.</AbstractText>
          <AbstractText Label="METHODS" NlmCategory="METHODS">To develop a curated training dataset with reduced biases, 46,947 chest X-ray images from various adult datasets were meticulously selected. Two preprocessing approaches were tried to assess the impact of thoracic segmentation on model attention outside the thoracic area. Evaluation of our approach was carried out on a dataset containing 5,856 chest X-rays of children from 1 to 5 years old.</AbstractText>
          <AbstractText Label="RESULTS" NlmCategory="RESULTS">An analysis of attention maps indicated that networks trained with thorax segmentation placed less attention on regions outside the thorax, thus eliminating potential bias. The ensuing network exhibited impressive performance when evaluated on an adult dataset, achieving a pneumonia discrimination AUC of 0.95. When tested on a pediatric dataset, the pneumonia discrimination AUC reached 0.82.</AbstractText>
          <AbstractText Label="CONCLUSIONS" NlmCategory="CONCLUSIONS">The results of this study show that adult-trained CNNs can be effectively applied to pediatric populations. This could potentially shift focus towards validating adult models over pediatric population instead of training new CNNs with limited pediatric data. To ensure the generalizability of deep learning models, it is important to implement techniques aimed at minimizing biases, such as image segmentation or low-quality image exclusion.</AbstractText>
